questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with low mood takes 20 paracetamol 500 mg tablets in one go. She has been taking St John's wort for 3 months. She does not drink alcohol, has a BMI of 24 and takes no other medicines. She is well, with normal observations.
questions.q: Which factor most increases her risk of liver injury?
questions.e: St John's wort induces P450 enzymes, increasing production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI and raising the risk of hepatotoxicity.

steps.x: The only enzyme-inducing factor in the stem.

elim: A normal BMI; malnutrition and anorexia raise the risk.
Not a recognised risk factor for paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
Explains why she overdosed but does not change liver risk.
A single timed ingestion is less risky than a staggered overdose.

steps.x: E: St John's wort. P450 inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort), alcohol, malnutrition, anorexia and HIV raise paracetamol risk.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted after taking 16 paracetamol 500 mg tablets. Her BMI is 14.8. She does not drink alcohol and takes no regular medicines. Her pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 92/60 mmHg. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which feature most increases her risk of hepatotoxicity?
questions.e: Malnutrition and anorexia deplete hepatic glutathione, so NAPQI accumulates at lower doses.

steps.x: Severe malnutrition.

elim: Reflects her starvation, not a direct liver risk factor.
Not a recognised risk factor for paracetamol liver injury.
8 g is significant, but her low glutathione stores make even this dose more dangerous.
Age is not a recognised risk factor.

steps.x: C: Malnutrition from anorexia nervosa. Anorexia, malnutrition, HIV, alcohol and P450 inducers increase paracetamol risk.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer is found very drowsy by a carer. Her daughter has been applying her pain patches and found several on her back. Her pupils are pinpoint. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm, BP 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 6 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Several fentanyl patches cause the opioid triad: reduced consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils.

steps.x: Too many opioid patches; pinpoint pupils and slow breathing.

elim: Causes dilated pupils and tachycardia.
Does not usually cause pinpoint pupils.
Does not cause drowsiness or pinpoint pupils early.
Causes tachypnoea, not respiratory depression.

steps.x: C: Fentanyl. Pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + low GCS = opioid toxidrome.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man is brought in by his partner, who found him sleepy with an empty packet of temazepam. He is rousable but slurs his speech and cannot walk without falling. His pupils are normal size and reactive. His pulse rate is 78 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 11 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Breath alcohol is zero.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sedation, slurred speech and ataxia with mild respiratory depression and normal pupils fit benzodiazepine toxicity.

steps.x: Sedation, ataxia, slurred speech, normal pupils.

elim: His breath alcohol is zero.
Possible with ataxia, but sedation and an empty temazepam packet point to overdose.
Causes pinpoint pupils; his pupils are normal.
Causes tachycardia, dilated pupils and a wide QRS.

steps.x: B: Benzodiazepine overdose. Benzodiazepine: drowsiness, ataxia, slurred speech, respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman says she took a large number of her mother's aspirin tablets 2 hours ago. She has ringing in her ears and has vomited. She is breathing deeply. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her arterial blood gas?
questions.e: Early aspirin toxicity stimulates the respiratory centre, giving a respiratory alkalosis (pH above 7.35) before metabolic acidosis develops.

steps.x: Early aspirin overdose: tinnitus, hyperventilation, high pH, low PaCO2.

elim: Develops later as salicylate accumulates; her pH is high.
Her bicarbonate is not raised; the low PaCO2 drives the alkalosis.
Her pH is high and PaCO2 low.
Needs a raised PaCO2; hers is low.

steps.x: E: Respiratory alkalosis. Aspirin: early respiratory alkalosis, then metabolic acidosis; tinnitus is the earliest symptom.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with chronic back pain is brought in drowsy after a day of vomiting. He complains of ringing in his ears and difficulty hearing. He is sweaty and breathing rapidly. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tinnitus, deafness, vomiting, sweating and hyperventilation with a metabolic acidosis is salicylate toxicity progressing from the early respiratory alkalosis.

steps.x: Tinnitus plus a high anion gap acidosis with normal glucose.

elim: His glucose is normal and ketones are negative.
Does not cause tinnitus, hearing loss or early acidosis.
Does not explain tinnitus and deafness.
Causes anticholinergic features and a wide QRS, not tinnitus.

steps.x: C: Salicylate toxicity. Aspirin: tinnitus first, then vomiting, dehydration and metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with depression has taken 30 of her amitriptyline 50 mg tablets. She is drowsy, flushed and has dilated pupils and dry skin. Her pulse rate is 134 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. A 12-lead ECG is recorded.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the ECG?
questions.e: TCAs block cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS (with PR and QT prolongation); QRS over 100 ms predicts seizures.

steps.x: TCA overdose with anticholinergic features.

elim: A sign of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
A sign of hyperkalaemia.
Seen in pre-excitation; TCAs prolong the PR interval.
A sign of hypothermia.

steps.x: D: Prolonged QRS duration. TCA ECG: sinus tachycardia with a wide QRS, long PR and QT.

questions.stem: A 55 year old farmer collapses after spraying crops without protective equipment. He is drooling, sweating heavily and has had diarrhoea. His chest is wheezy with copious secretions. His pupils are pinpoint. His pulse rate is 44 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which toxidrome is most likely?
questions.e: Salivation, sweating, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia and pinpoint pupils are the cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphate exposure.

steps.x: Organophosphate exposure with secretions everywhere.

elim: Hot, dry and tachycardic with dilated pupils; the opposite picture.
Pinpoint pupils, but with a slow respiratory rate and no secretions or diarrhoea.
Causes drowsiness and ataxia without secretions.
Tachycardic and hypertensive with dilated pupils.

steps.x: B: Cholinergic. Cholinergic: salivation, sweating, diarrhoea, pinpoint pupils, bronchorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has central chest pain and palpitations 1 hour after snorting a white powder at a party. He is agitated and sweating. His pupils are dilated. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 136 bpm, BP 182/104 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which drug has he most likely taken?
questions.e: Agitation, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia and dilated pupils are the sympathomimetic toxidrome; snorted powder with chest pain suggests cocaine.

steps.x: Sympathomimetic toxidrome plus chest pain.

elim: Anticholinergic: dry skin rather than sweating, and not snorted at parties.
Causes sedation, not agitation and hypertension.
Causes pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression.
Causes a cholinergic picture with pinpoint pupils and bradycardia.

steps.x: B: Cocaine. Sympathomimetic: sweaty, agitated, tachycardic, hypertensive, dilated pupils (cocaine, amphetamines).

questions.stem: An 81 year old man with mild dementia lives alone and takes amlodipine, ramipril and bisoprolol from a weekly pill organiser. His daughter visits and finds he has taken the whole week's tablets over 2 days because he forgot he had taken them. He is dizzy. His pulse rate is 46 bpm and BP 84/48 mmHg.
questions.q: Which best describes this overdose?
questions.e: Overdose can be accidental, intentional, recreational or a therapeutic misadventure; taking extra prescribed doses in error is therapeutic misadventure.

steps.x: Prescribed medicines taken in excess by mistake.

elim: He took them by mistake, not to harm himself.
The problem is too much of his usual drugs, not an interaction.
He has taken too much, not had an unpredictable reaction to a normal dose.
These are prescribed medicines taken in error.

steps.x: E: Therapeutic misadventure. Overdose types: accidental, intentional, recreational, therapeutic misadventure.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman is found collapsed with an empty packet of her father's atenolol beside her. She is drowsy and cold. Her pulse rate is 36 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her pupils are normal. Capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and reduced consciousness after atenolol is beta-blocker toxicity.

steps.x: Marked bradycardia, hypotension, low glucose.

elim: Causes sedation but not profound bradycardia and hypotension.
Causes pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression.
Causes tachycardia, tachypnoea and tinnitus.
Causes tachycardia and dilated pupils.

steps.x: B: Beta-blocker overdose. Beta-blocker overdose: bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with atrial fibrillation on warfarin has extensive bruising on her arms and nosebleeds for 2 days. She recently started taking an extra tablet each day, thinking it would help her heart. She is alert. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm irregular and BP 138/80 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
questions.e: Extra warfarin tablets with an INR of 8.6 and a normal platelet count is warfarin overdose.

steps.x: Excess warfarin, very high INR, normal platelets.

elim: Needs a trigger such as sepsis, with low platelets.
Congenital and presents in childhood with a prolonged APTT.
Her platelets are normal.
No features of liver disease and the history points to extra warfarin.

steps.x: E: Warfarin overdose. Bleeding on warfarin with a high INR = warfarin toxicity; vitamin K reverses it.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes is found drowsy by his wife with empty packets of several medicines. He is sweaty and responds only to voice. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His airway is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate bedside investigation?
questions.e: A drowsy, sweaty diabetic patient after an overdose may be hypoglycaemic; a capillary glucose is the first bedside check.

steps.x: Reduced consciousness in a diabetic who may have overdosed.

elim: Not a bedside test and not urgent with normal breathing.
Considered later; reversible causes come first.
Needed, but not a bedside test and it does not explain drowsiness now.
Slow and rarely changes immediate management.

steps.x: A: Capillary blood glucose. Bedside tests first: capillary glucose, ECG, observations and blood gas.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman says she has taken "a handful" of tablets from the medicine cabinet 2 hours ago but does not know what they were. She is alert and talking. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which additional bedside investigation is mandatory?
questions.e: An ECG is mandatory in every overdose to look for cardiotoxicity (QRS, QT, arrhythmias), even when the patient looks well.

clues: does not know what they were
steps.x: Unknown drugs, glucose already checked.

elim: Not routine in a well patient after overdose.
Not relevant to overdose.
Not relevant to overdose.
Does not identify cardiotoxic drugs.

steps.x: A: 12-lead ECG. Every overdose: capillary glucose and a mandatory ECG.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman took 32 paracetamol 500 mg tablets at one time, 6 hours before arriving in the emergency department. She weighs 60 kg. She has nausea but no abdominal pain. Her observations are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Paracetamol level now, plotted on the treatment nomogram
questions.e: Levels taken from 4 hours after a single ingestion can be plotted; she is at 6 hours, so take the level now and plot it.

steps.x: Single timed ingestion, already more than 4 hours.

elim: LFTs are often normal early; the level decides treatment.
16 g is a potentially fatal dose.
She is already past 4 hours; waiting delays treatment.
Does not give a level to plot on the nomogram.

steps.x: D: Paracetamol level now, plotted on the treatment nomogram. Paracetamol level from 4 hours after ingestion, plotted on the nomogram.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has taken 40 dosulepin tablets. He is drowsy, tachycardic and has dry skin and dilated pupils. His 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 128 bpm with a QRS duration of 116 ms. His BP is 108/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which complication is this QRS duration most associated with?
questions.e: In TCA overdose a QRS over 100 ms is associated with seizures and over 160 ms with ventricular arrhythmias, so the ECG is the most important test.

steps.x: TCA with QRS between 100 and 160 ms.

elim: A feature of paracetamol, not TCA, toxicity.
Not linked to QRS duration.
Not linked to QRS duration in TCA toxicity.
Linked to a QRS over 160 ms; his is 116 ms.

steps.x: D: Seizures. QRS >100 ms = seizure risk; >160 ms = ventricular arrhythmia risk.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man is brought in by ambulance after his wife found him confused with several empty blister packs. He has no airway or breathing problem. His pupils are dilated, skin dry and pulse rate 118 bpm. A junior doctor asks how the diagnosis of drug toxicity is confirmed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach?
o: Clinical assessment with targeted drug-specific tests
CT head as the definitive test
questions.e: The gold standard is clinical assessment (history, toxidrome, observations, ECG) plus drug-specific tests guided by the suspected drug, such as paracetamol or salicylate levels.

clues: how the diagnosis of drug toxicity is confirmed
steps.x: Toxidrome clues plus empty packets.

elim: Excludes structural causes but does not confirm poisoning.
Does not identify drug toxicity.
For infection; it does not confirm poisoning.
Detects only some drugs and does not show the dose or toxicity.

steps.x: A: Clinical assessment with targeted drug-specific tests. Gold standard: clinical assessment plus targeted drug testing.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man is brought to the emergency department unresponsive after taking an unknown quantity of tablets. He is making loud snoring noises. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. His GCS is 7.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in management?
questions.e: ABCDE comes first: snoring with a GCS of 7 shows a partly obstructed airway that must be opened and protected before anything else.

steps.x: Airway obstruction in an unconscious patient.

elim: Mandatory, but airway comes first in ABCDE.
Never in an unprotected airway; aspiration risk.
Part of D; airway comes first.
Needed later; they do not treat the immediate threat.

steps.x: D: Open and support the airway. ABCDE always first: airway (protect if unconscious), breathing, circulation, disability, exposure.

questions.stem: A 20 year old student phones 111. Her flatmate has taken a large number of tablets and is now unconscious on the floor. She is breathing normally and has a pulse. An ambulance has been called. The call handler gives first aid advice while help is on the way.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Give her salt water to make her vomit
Leave her on her back and wait
Place her in the recovery position
Sit her upright in a chair
questions.e: Unconscious but breathing normally: recovery position. Not breathing normally: call 999 and start CPR.

clues: breathing normally and has a pulse
steps.x: Unconscious, breathing, help on the way.

elim: Inducing vomiting is dangerous and not advised.
She may obstruct her airway or aspirate.
An unconscious person cannot hold her airway sitting up.
CPR is for someone not breathing normally; she is breathing.

steps.x: C: Place her in the recovery position. Unconscious but breathing = recovery position; not breathing normally = CPR.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is found drowsy at home. In the emergency department his airway, breathing and circulation have been assessed and supported. His GCS is 12 and capillary glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. His pupils are pinpoint. On exposure, three transdermal patches are found on his back.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Exposure in ABCDE looks for patches, needle marks and pill packets; removing the patches stops further absorption, with naloxone if needed.

steps.x: E of ABCDE finds the source of opioid.

elim: Does not work for transdermal absorption and is unsafe with reduced GCS.
Not used; the drug is coming through the skin.
Reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
The patches and pinpoint pupils explain his drowsiness.

steps.x: D: Remove the patches. Exposure: look for patches, needle marks, pill packets and toxidrome clues.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man on a methadone programme is found unresponsive with a respiratory rate of 5 breaths per minute and pinpoint pupils. He wakes fully after 400 micrograms of IV naloxone. Forty minutes later he becomes drowsy again with a respiratory rate of 7 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Repeat naloxone and start a naloxone infusion
questions.e: Naloxone is a short-acting competitive mu-receptor antagonist; long-acting opioids like methadone outlast it, so repeat doses or an infusion are needed.

clues: Forty minutes later he becomes drowsy again
steps.x: Re-sedation after naloxone wears off.

elim: Methadone outlasts naloxone; he would re-sedate.
Reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
Used for maintenance after detoxification, not acute reversal.
His re-sedation is explained by long-acting methadone.

steps.x: D: Repeat naloxone and start a naloxone infusion. Naloxone for opioid overdose; long-acting opioids need repeated doses or an infusion.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman is given IV midazolam for sedation during an endoscopy. Ten minutes later she cannot be roused and her respiratory rate falls to 6 breaths per minute despite airway support. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on oxygen. She takes no regular medicines and has no history of seizures.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
questions.e: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine overdose; iatrogenic sedation in a patient without seizures or benzodiazepine dependence is its classic use.

steps.x: Benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression.

elim: For bradycardia or beta-blocker overdose.
Reverses opioids; she has had a benzodiazepine.
For TCA or salicylate toxicity.
She cannot protect her airway, and midazolam was given IV.

steps.x: B: Intravenous flumazenil. Flumazenil for benzodiazepine overdose.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man took 30 propranolol 80 mg tablets 2 hours ago. He is drowsy. His pulse rate is 38 bpm, BP 76/42 mmHg and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. His airway is patent and he is on oxygen. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus bradycardia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: Beta-blocker overdose with bradycardia and hypotension is treated with IV atropine, adding glucagon if resistant.

steps.x: Symptomatic bradycardia from beta-blockade.

elim: Slows the heart further; used for SVT.
For benzodiazepine overdose.
For opioid overdose.
Another beta-blocker; it would worsen toxicity.

steps.x: B: Intravenous atropine. Beta-blocker overdose: atropine, then glucagon if resistant.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve has an INR of 9.2 after taking double doses by mistake for a week. He has gum bleeding and widespread bruising but no major bleeding. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 128 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue warfarin at the same dose
Withhold warfarin and give IV vitamin K
questions.e: Warfarin overdose with minor bleeding: stop warfarin and give IV vitamin K; add prothrombin complex concentrate for major bleeding.

steps.x: Very high INR with minor bleeding.

elim: His INR is dangerously high and he is bleeding.
Reverses heparin, not warfarin.
Does not reverse the warfarin effect.
DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.

steps.x: E: Withhold warfarin and give IV vitamin K. Vitamin K reverses warfarin.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman took 40 paracetamol 500 mg tablets 45 minutes ago and came straight to hospital. She weighs 58 kg and is alert with a GCS of 15. Her observations are normal and she has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Within 1 hour of a significant paracetamol ingestion, give activated charcoal to reduce absorption; she is alert so her airway is safe. NAC follows based on the level.

steps.x: Large paracetamol dose within 1 hour, alert.

elim: Not recommended routinely; charcoal is used within 1 hour.
For benzodiazepine overdose.
For opioid overdose.
For salicylate or TCA toxicity.

steps.x: E: Oral activated charcoal. Paracetamol: activated charcoal within 1 hour, then NAC as indicated.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman is receiving the first bag of IV acetylcysteine for a paracetamol overdose. Twenty minutes in she develops flushing, an itchy urticarial rash and mild wheeze. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There is no stridor or facial swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Give IM adrenaline and stop NAC permanently
Increase the infusion rate to finish faster
Stop NAC permanently and monitor LFTs only
Stop the infusion and give IV chlorphenamine
questions.e: A non-IgE anaphylactoid reaction to NAC: stop the infusion, give 10 mg IV chlorphenamine (and nebulised salbutamol), then restart at a slower rate.

steps.x: Mild anaphylactoid reaction to NAC.

elim: This is an anaphylactoid reaction without shock; NAC is restarted once settled.
Reactions are rate-related; this worsens them.
She still needs NAC to protect her liver.
Not the standard UK treatment; NAC is restarted.

steps.x: D: Stop the infusion and give IV chlorphenamine. NAC reaction: stop, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV, restart slower.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man is found confused at home by his brother, with empty packets of paracetamol. He cannot say when or how many he took. He drinks 50 units of alcohol a week. His observations are normal. His blood tests have just been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Discharge if the paracetamol level is undetectable
Repeat the paracetamol level in 4 hours
Wait for the paracetamol level before deciding
questions.e: When ingestion time is unknown or staggered, the nomogram cannot be used; start NAC immediately regardless of the level, especially with chronic alcohol use.

clues: cannot say when or how many
steps.x: Unknown time of ingestion, high-risk drinker.

elim: Levels can be low after a delayed or staggered overdose with liver injury.
Time of ingestion is unknown, so charcoal is unlikely to help.
The nomogram cannot be used without a known ingestion time.
Delay worsens outcome; NAC starts now.

steps.x: D: Start IV acetylcysteine immediately. Unknown or staggered paracetamol overdose = immediate NAC regardless of level.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has completed the standard course of IV acetylcysteine for a paracetamol overdose taken 26 hours ago. Repeat bloods are taken at the end of the infusion. She feels well. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: NAC is continued while the paracetamol concentration or ALT remains elevated, continuing to replenish glutathione.

steps.x: End of NAC, but ALT rising and paracetamol still detectable.

elim: Her ALT is rising and the paracetamol is still detectable.
Only useful within 1 hour of ingestion.
She has no features of acute liver failure yet.
Her INR is only slightly raised; it does not replace NAC.

steps.x: A: Continue acetylcysteine. Continue NAC if paracetamol or ALT remain elevated.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman took 70 aspirin 300 mg tablets 6 hours ago. She has tinnitus and has vomited. She is alert with a clear chest. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Her kidney function is normal. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Moderate salicylate toxicity is treated with urinary alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate; haemodialysis is kept for pulmonary oedema or severe acidosis.

steps.x: Moderate salicylate level, no pulmonary oedema, normal kidneys.

elim: She is past 1 hour, and her salicylate level needs active elimination.
For severe toxicity with pulmonary oedema, severe acidosis or very high levels.
For paracetamol overdose.
For opioid overdose.

steps.x: E: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Aspirin: charcoal within 1 h, IV bicarbonate (urinary alkalinisation), dialysis if severe.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man took 50 paracetamol tablets 3 days ago and did not seek help. He now has right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. His ALT is 6800 IU/L and INR 3.8. A liver biopsy is not needed, but a student asks what is happening in the liver.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his liver injury?
questions.e: Overdose depletes hepatic glutathione, so the toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulates and causes centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis.

clues: right upper quadrant pain and jaundice
steps.x: Late paracetamol overdose with acute liver injury.

elim: Describes autoimmune hepatitis.
Gives a cholestatic picture, not an ALT of 6800.
The parent drug is safe; its metabolite is toxic.
Does not explain a paracetamol overdose with massive ALT rise.

steps.x: D: NAPQI accumulation after glutathione depletion. Paracetamol: glutathione depleted, NAPQI accumulates, centrilobular necrosis.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man took a large aspirin overdose 14 hours ago. His first blood gas showed pH 7.50 and PaCO2 3.2 kPa. His latest gas shows pH 7.22, PaCO2 3.4 kPa and bicarbonate 10 mmol/L with a raised lactate. A student asks why the acidosis has developed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his metabolic acidosis?
o: Direct stimulation of the respiratory centre
questions.e: Accumulating salicylate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, so lactic and organic acids build up and a metabolic acidosis is superimposed on the respiratory alkalosis.

steps.x: Early alkalosis, now metabolic acidosis.

elim: Explains the early respiratory alkalosis, not the later acidosis.
His PaCO2 is low; he is hyperventilating.
Describes diabetic ketoacidosis.
Gives a normal anion gap acidosis; he has a raised lactate.

steps.x: E: Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. Aspirin: respiratory centre stimulation early; uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation later.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has taken 35 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets. Her 12-lead ECG shows a QRS duration of 148 ms. Her pulse rate is 132 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg. A student asks why the QRS complex has widened.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Blockade of fast sodium channels in cardiac myocytes
Calcium channel blockade at the AV node
questions.e: TCAs block cardiac sodium channels, slowing phase 0 depolarisation and widening the QRS.

steps.x: TCA with a wide QRS.

elim: Prolongs the QT interval, not mainly the QRS.
Causes bradycardia and AV block, as in verapamil toxicity.
TCAs are anticholinergic, reducing vagal tone.
This is how digoxin works.

steps.x: A: Blockade of fast sodium channels in cardiac myocytes. TCA cardiotoxicity = sodium channel blockade, slow phase 0, wide QRS.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with amitriptyline overdose has a QRS duration of 132 ms and BP 84/50 mmHg. He is given 50 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate IV. Ten minutes later the QRS has narrowed to 104 ms and his BP is 98/60 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this improvement?
o: Bicarbonate binds amitriptyline in the gut
Bicarbonate increases renal excretion of amitriptyline
Raised extracellular sodium and alkalaemia improve sodium channel function
questions.e: Sodium bicarbonate raises extracellular sodium and alkalinises the blood, which reduces TCA binding to sodium channels, narrows the QRS and lowers arrhythmia risk.

steps.x: QRS narrowed after bicarbonate.

elim: Given IV; it does not bind the drug.
It has no anticholinergic action.
TCAs are not significantly cleared this way.
Alkalinisation lowers potassium; that is not the benefit.

steps.x: E: Raised extracellular sodium and alkalaemia improve sodium channel function. TCA: IV bicarbonate (sodium load and alkalinisation), ECG monitoring, senior input.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman is found unresponsive after injecting heroin. Her respiratory rate is 4 breaths per minute and her pupils are pinpoint. Within 1 minute of IV naloxone she is awake and breathing at 16 breaths per minute. A student asks why the heroin stopped her breathing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her respiratory depression?
o: Blockade of nicotinic receptors at the diaphragm
Mu-opioid receptor agonism in the brainstem
questions.e: Opioids depress breathing by agonism at mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem respiratory centres; naloxone competitively blocks these receptors.

steps.x: Rapid reversal by naloxone.

elim: Describes neuromuscular blockers.
How benzodiazepines cause sedation.
How organophosphates cause a cholinergic toxidrome.
Opioids are agonists; antagonism would not suppress breathing.

steps.x: E: Mu-opioid receptor agonism in the brainstem. Opioids: mu agonists in the brainstem; naloxone: competitive mu antagonist.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man drinks an organophosphate pesticide. He has profuse salivation, sweating, diarrhoea, wheeze with copious secretions, pinpoint pupils and a pulse rate of 42 bpm. A student asks why so many body systems are affected in the same way.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his features?
questions.e: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at every cholinergic synapse; one shared receptor system explains the recognisable toxidrome.

steps.x: Cholinergic excess everywhere.

elim: Gives the opposite (anticholinergic) picture: dry, hot, tachycardic.
Gives pinpoint pupils but no secretions or diarrhoea.
Causes a sympathomimetic picture.
Causes a wide QRS, as in TCA toxicity.

steps.x: B: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Toxidromes reflect a toxin class acting on a shared receptor system.
